answer.sourceLine: Matthew 5:4, the second Beatitude of the Sermon on the Mount, where the words are spoken by Jesus. This exact English wording is the King James Version’s, published in 1611, and is confirmed word for word in the Project Gutenberg KJV text ↗.

source.excerpt: And seeing the multitudes, he went up into a mountain: and when he was set, his disciples came unto him: And he opened his mouth, and taught them, saying, Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted. Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.
trail: Primary text: the Project Gutenberg King James Version ↗ reads, at Matthew 5:4, “Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted.” Wikisource’s KJV transcription ↗ has the same words.
The translation: according to Wikipedia ↗, the King James Version “was commissioned in 1604 and published in 1611, by sponsorship of King James VI and I.”

The earlier English rendering: William Tyndale’s New Testament, first published complete in 1526 according to Wikipedia ↗, already reads “Blessed are they that morne: for they shalbe conforted” (Tyndale text at BibleStudyTools ↗). The KJV kept it almost word for word.
The Greek and its parallel: Wikipedia’s Matthew 5:4 article ↗ gives the Greek text and notes the verse is often seen as a version of Luke 6:21 from the Sermon on the Plain.
source.excerptNote: Matthew 5:1–5, King James Version, as transcribed in the Project Gutenberg edition.
source.rightsNote: The wording is the King James Version, published in 1611, so it is public domain in the United States. In the UK the KJV is still under the Crown’s perpetual rights; Wikipedia ↗ describes it as “Perpetually copyrighted in UK” and “De facto public domain elsewhere.” Modern translations of this verse are separate works and may be under copyright.

author.metaLine: c. 80–90 AD · Anonymous Gospel, traditionally credited to Matthew the Apostle
author.bio: The first book of the New Testament, written in Koine Greek. According to Wikipedia ↗, it was written “in the last quarter of the first century anonymously by a Jewish author,” and tradition credits it to Matthew the Apostle. Its first long discourse is the Sermon on the Mount, which opens with the Beatitudes.

misattribution.heading: Who else gets the credit
misattribution.intro: The line is genuine scripture, but the credit for it travels in a few different directions depending on who is quoting it.

items.why: In Matthew’s narrative these are Jesus’s words. He opens his mouth and teaches his disciples on the mountain (Matthew 5:1–2, KJV ↗). Crediting Jesus names the speaker, and crediting Matthew names the written source. Both are fair.

Quotewise ↗ credits the line to Tyndale and names no edition. Tyndale did translate the verse into English (“Blessed are they that morne: for they shalbe conforted,” BibleStudyTools ↗), and the KJV wording follows his closely. But he translated the Gospel; he did not write the saying.

items.who: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted”
items.why: Newer Bibles word the verse differently. The World English Bible has “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Wikipedia ↗). These are the same verse, not separate quotations. The “they that mourn” form is the KJV’s.
Luke’s Sermon on the Plain has a related Beatitude, “Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh” (Wikipedia ↗). It is a different wording, and “they that mourn” comes from Matthew.

misattribution.truthLine: The exact words “Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted” are Matthew 5:4 in the 1611 King James Version, where Jesus speaks them in the Sermon on the Mount (Bible Gateway ↗).

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: This is the second of the Beatitudes, the blessings that open the Sermon on the Mount. Wikipedia’s Matthew 5:4 article ↗ notes that some scholars read the verse against Isaiah 61, and that in several early versions verses 4 and 5 appear in reverse order.

The familiar English cadence is older than the King James Version. Tyndale’s translation already had “Blessed are they that morne: for they shalbe conforted,” and the 1611 translators kept it nearly unchanged. Scholars cited by Wikipedia ↗ say the KJV owed most of its New Testament to Tyndale.
